transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, it's... it's a lot of things, really, but I suppose if I had to boil it down, I just don't feel like myself anymore. I mean, I've been working as a janitor over at the community college for going on fifteen years now, and usually, I'm the kind of guy who says hello to everyone in the halls, you know? I'd chat with the professors, the students, even the delivery guys. But lately, I just... I barely talk to anyone. I don't want to. It's like I just go completely flat and quiet inside. People will say good morning, and I just kind of stare at them, or I mumble something and walk away. I don't have the energy for it. And it's not just the talking. Just doing the job itself... getting started on my cleaning route every evening feels like I'm trying to push a loaded supply cart up a steep hill in the mud. I just stand there looking at the mop bucket and the trash bags, and I can't seem to make my arms and legs do what they're supposed to do. It takes everything I have just to put one foot in front of the other, and even then, I feel like I'm moving in slow motion. I used to take pride in getting the floors to shine, but now, I just don't care, and I don't have the drive to even try. It's just... it's all so heavy, Doctor. Everything is just so heavy and empty all at once.
Have you been seeing or hearing things that others around you do not seem to notice?

Well, it's funny you ask that, Doctor, because... well, actually it's not funny at all, it's been really throwing me off on top of everything else. You see, I work the evening shift, right? So by the time I get to the main corridors, especially over in the older buildings on campus, most of the students and the faculty are long gone. It gets real quiet in there. Usually it's just the hum of the vending machines and the squeak of my shoes on the linoleum. 

But lately... I’ll be out there mopping after hours. Just pushing the mop, trying to get through the night like I was telling you, feeling like I'm dragging a hundred pounds. And right when I'm near the main stairwell—the one with the heavy double doors—I'll hear this voice. It’s a man’s voice, real deep, and it is just as clear as you and me talking right now. He'll say my name. Just out of nowhere. Or sometimes he'll tell me I've missed a spot. 

I swear to you, it sounds like he is standing right there by the stairwell, just watching me work. The first time it happened, I actually stopped and leaned on my mop handle and called out, because I figured it was the night security guard making his rounds, or maybe a professor who stayed late to grade papers. I walked right over to the stairwell, and I pulled the door open, and I looked up and down the steps... and there was nobody. Not a single soul. 

And it just keeps happening. I'll be totally alone, the exterior doors are all locked, I know for an absolute fact I'm the only one in that wing of the building, and I'll hear him again. "You missed a spot." It really gives me a fright, you know? I just stand there holding the mop, staring at the empty space, and my heart starts pounding. I try to tell myself maybe it's just the acoustics of the building, because it does echo in those old halls, sure, but an echo has to come from somewhere, right? It has to be a real person making the noise to begin with. But when I look, there is never, ever anybody there. I just don't understand it.
Have you ever experienced these voices or felt this heavy, empty state during times in your life when you were not feeling this deeply depressed?

Well, that's... that's an interesting question, Dr. Smith, because I've thought about that myself. You know, trying to make sense of it all. I keep a little calendar in my locker at work—just one of those free ones you get from the bank—and I try to mark down when things are really bad, just so I can keep track. And there was a time, not too long ago, maybe a couple of months back, where that heavy feeling... that feeling like I was walking through wet cement all the time, it actually lifted a bit. It wasn't perfect, I wasn't doing cartwheels down the hallway or anything, but for a stretch of, oh, maybe three or four weeks, I was actually getting through my shifts without feeling completely exhausted. I was eating my dinner—usually I just bring a turkey sandwich and an apple, maybe some potato chips if they're on sale—and I was actually finishing it, instead of just staring at it and throwing it in the breakroom trash. I felt... well, I felt a little more like myself. 

But the thing is, Doctor, even during those weeks when my mood was better and I had a little more energy, the other stuff didn't stop. I still heard that voice. I'd be sweeping near the stairwell, feeling okay, maybe even humming a little tune to myself, and clear as day, "You missed a spot," or he'd just say my name. "Gary." Just like that. And I still knew—I mean, I was absolutely convinced—that the security cameras in the hallways were tracking me. We have these little dome cameras, they put them in about five years ago, and I swear they follow me. I’ll move from the water fountain to the supply closet, and I can feel the lens shifting. Even when I was feeling pretty decent, eating my sandwiches, pushing the cart without feeling like I was dying, I still knew those cameras were watching my every move, and I still heard that man in the stairwell. So, yes, it seems like even when the darkness backs off a little, those other things... they just stay right there with me. It’s very unsettling, to tell you the truth, because you'd think if you felt better, everything would get better, right? But it just doesn't seem to work that way for me.
Looking back at that calendar you mentioned, how long have you been dealing with these experiences—the voice in the stairwell and the feeling that the cameras are following you—in total?

Well, you know, Dr. Smith, that calendar... it's funny how time just sort of slips away from you when you work the night shift. You start measuring the year by the college semesters instead of regular months. Like, there's the fall rush, and then the winter break where the campus turns into a total ghost town, and then the spring thaw. But looking back at the dates I circled—because I use a red pen for the really strange days, just a standard red ballpoint I found left behind in one of the lecture halls, I always keep it right there in my shirt pocket—I've been tracking it pretty closely. 

If I trace it all the way back to the very first time I heard that deep voice by the heavy double doors, and when I first started noticing the lenses on those dome cameras shifting to track my supply cart... it’s been about eleven months now. Eleven whole months of this. I remember specifically because it started right around the time we were doing the mid-semester deep cleans last year, and I had to order a whole new batch of floor wax from the supplier. I actually thought maybe the fumes from the floor stripper were getting to my head at first, you know? Because we have to use the industrial grade stuff for the scuff marks the kids leave. But the stripping and waxing only lasted a week, and the voice... well, the voice and the cameras just kept right on going. Every single month, right through the holidays, right through the spring, and here we are now, eleven months later, and he's still telling me I missed a spot. It's just exhausting, Doctor, carrying that around for nearly a whole year. You'd think a person would get used to it after all that time, but you really don't. Every time I hear him, it's just as startling as the very first night.

Over the past eleven months, would you say that the periods where you felt that heavy, depressed mood lasted for most of the time, or were they relatively short compared to the times you felt more like yourself?

Well, if I really sit down and think about it... and I do think about it a lot, especially when I'm just sitting in the breakroom staring at the wall instead of eating my sandwich... I'd have to say the heavy periods are definitely the rule, not the exception. 

You see, ever since the move—I had to pack up and move into this smaller apartment across town right around the time all this started eleven months ago, which was just a tremendous hassle, hauling all those boxes by myself with my bad knees—but for most of the time since that move, it's just been this constant weight. The sadness, the low energy... it's just always there. And the guilt, too. I feel this awful guilt that I can't just snap out of it and be a normal, productive person, you know? I used to love tinkering with old radios on my days off, fixing up the wiring, listening to the static clear up. But I've had this complete loss of interest in all of it. I haven't even turned on the desk lamp at my workbench in months. The tools are just gathering dust.

And the really frustrating part, Dr. Smith, the thing that really wears a man down, is that it never really goes away. Even on the days when that deep voice in the stairwell is just relentless, or when my worries about those dome cameras watching me are the absolute main thing on my mind—like when I'm so focused on the lenses tracking my supply cart that my hands are actually sweating on the mop handle—even then, the sadness and that drained, empty feeling are still right there in the background. 

You'd think being terrified of someone watching you would kind of snap you out of being depressed, wouldn't you? Like adrenaline or something would take over. But it doesn't work like that. It’s like a heavy, wet blanket underneath everything else. So, yes, even when the strange things are happening and taking up all my attention, the low energy and the guilt are still just humming right along in the background, for most of the time. It really never gives me a break.

During these past eleven months, have there ever been any stretches of time, lasting at least two weeks, where you were completely free of those heavy, depressed feelings, but the voice and the suspicion about the cameras were still happening?

Well, yes, exactly, Dr. Smith. It's just like I was mentioning a little bit ago when we first started talking today... you're hitting the nail right on the head, or maybe I'm just repeating myself, but yes. 

There was that specific stretch of several weeks—definitely more than two weeks, I'd say closer to three or maybe even four—where my mood had actually lifted some. I remember it clear as day because it was just such a tremendous relief not to feel like I was dragging a hundred-pound weight chained to my ankle every time I had to walk down the corridor. I was getting through my meals, actually eating that turkey sandwich I told you about instead of just tossing it in the bin, and I was getting through my work a little better, too. The floor buffer didn't feel nearly as heavy, and I wasn't dreading the start of my shift the way I usually do. 

But—and this is the part that really just baffles me, I've spent hours thinking about it while I'm wiping down the baseboards—even though I wasn't feeling that awful, crushing depression, the other things didn't stop. I still heard my name in the stairwell. Just as loud and clear as ever, echoing off the concrete. And I stayed absolutely convinced that those hallway cameras were being used to track me. 

I'd be feeling fine, you know, relatively speaking, maybe even looking forward to going back to my apartment and putting my feet up, but I'd look up at that little black dome on the ceiling near the science labs, and I just knew... I knew in my bones that whoever was on the other side of that lens was following my cart. I could feel the motors in the camera adjusting to keep me in the frame. So, to answer your question, yes, there was absolutely a time, for several weeks there, where the heavy, empty feelings took a vacation, but the voice and the cameras didn't go anywhere at all. They just stayed right there on shift with me, completely uninterrupted. It’s a very strange place to be in mentally, I have to tell you, feeling okay but still having all that going on around you.

During your life, have you ever had any periods lasting at least a few days where you felt unusually energetic, didn't need much sleep, or felt so wired and 'on top of the world' that it was clearly different from your normal self?

Well, Dr. Smith, I can tell you right now, 'on top of the world' is definitely not a phrase anybody would ever use to describe me. Not even way back when I was younger, taking those business administration classes at the community college before I started doing the maintenance work. I mean... unusually energetic? I honestly don't think I've ever felt like that in my entire life. 

You ask about not needing much sleep, and, well, I wish I had that problem sometimes! Working the night shift, your sleep schedule gets all turned around and chopped up anyway. I usually try to get my solid seven or eight hours during the day, pulling the blackout curtains tight—I actually went out and bought these heavy-duty ones, the thick kind they use in those nice hotels downtown, because the morning sun just cuts right through my bedroom window and heats up the whole room. But even with those curtains, I'm just always tired. 

I've never had a time where I felt wired, or where I didn't need to sleep for days on end. My baseline is pretty much just... steady, slow, and worn out. Especially with my bad knees. Pushing that heavy supply cart around all night, hauling the giant industrial trash bags out to the main dumpsters behind the cafeteria... it takes every ounce of energy I have just to get through it. There's no bouncing off the walls for me, no big bursts of energy where I feel like I can conquer the world or anything like that. It's really just the exact opposite, like we were talking about before with that heavy, wet blanket feeling. So, no, I can safely say I’ve never experienced anything even close to what you're describing there. Just a whole lot of exhaustion, plain and simple.

Aside from the stretch of time you mentioned earlier, have there been any other periods in your life, lasting at least two weeks, where you experienced these voices or suspicious thoughts about the cameras while your mood was completely normal?

Well, let me really think back on that, Dr. Smith, because I do like to give you the most accurate answer I can. I spend a lot of time thinking about my life while I'm working. You know, when you're just walking up and down those long corridors, back and forth with the floor buffer, you have a lot of time to just chew on your own thoughts. 

And if I'm looking back over my whole life... no, I really don't think so. Because, like I was saying earlier, all this strange business—the voice in the stairwell, the absolute certainty about those dome cameras tracking my cart—all of that really only started up about eleven months ago, right around that awful move to the smaller apartment. Before that... well, I mean, I was always tired, sure, and my knees have been giving me grief for the better part of a decade from all the standing and hauling, but I never heard anyone calling my name when the halls were empty. And I certainly didn't pay any mind to the security cameras back then. I'd just dust the lenses if they got cobwebs on them and keep right on moving. 

So, since the strange things only started eleven months ago, I only have that window of time to look at. And in these past eleven months, it really was just that one specific stretch I told you about—those three or four weeks where the heavy, empty feeling took a vacation but the cameras and the voice stayed on shift. I've racked my brain, going back and forth over the calendar in my head while I'm emptying the recycling bins, trying to remember if maybe there was another time, maybe over the winter holidays? But no. It was just that one time. 

Every other day since this all began, if the voice is there, and if the cameras are watching me, that wet blanket of sadness and guilt is right there with them, wrapped around my shoulders. They've all just been bundled up together, day in and day out. I really wish there had been other times, I'll tell you that much, because feeling somewhat normal in your mood, even if you're terrified the cameras are following you, is a heck of a lot better than feeling so weighed down you can barely lift your arms to tie a trash bag... but no, just that one time.

patient.answer:
Well, if I really sit down and think about it... and I do think about it a lot, especially when I'm just sitting in the breakroom staring at the wall instead of eating my sandwich... I'd have to say the heavy periods are definitely the rule, not the exception. 

You see, ever since the move—I had to pack up and move into this smaller apartment across town right around the time all this started eleven months ago, which was just a tremendous hassle, hauling all those boxes by myself with my bad knees—but for most of the time since that move, it's just been this constant weight. The sadness, the low energy... it's just always there. And the guilt, too. I feel this awful guilt that I can't just snap out of it and be a normal, productive person, you know? I used to love tinkering with old radios on my days off, fixing up the wiring, listening to the static clear up. But I've had this complete loss of interest in all of it. I haven't even turned on the desk lamp at my workbench in months. The tools are just gathering dust.

And the really frustrating part, Dr. Smith, the thing that really wears a man down, is that it never really goes away. Even on the days when that deep voice in the stairwell is just relentless, or when my worries about those dome cameras watching me are the absolute main thing on my mind—like when I'm so focused on the lenses tracking my supply cart that my hands are actually sweating on the mop handle—even then, the sadness and that drained, empty feeling are still right there in the background. 

You'd think being terrified of someone watching you would kind of snap you out of being depressed, wouldn't you? Like adrenaline or something would take over. But it doesn't work like that. It’s like a heavy, wet blanket underneath everything else. So, yes, even when the strange things are happening and taking up all my attention, the low energy and the guilt are still just humming right along in the background, for most of the time. It really never gives me a break.

inference.note: Ruled out F25.0 (Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type) because the patient reports a predominantly depressed mood rather than manic or mixed episodes. The symptoms have persisted for 11 months, with mood symptoms being the 'rule' and the primary feature accompanying the psychosis, keeping F20.0, F20.81, and F25.1 as viable candidates.

doctor.intent: Determine if the psychotic symptoms have ever occurred in the absence of a mood episode for a significant period, which is essential to distinguish Schizoaffective Disorder from Schizophrenia.
doctor.question: During these past eleven months, have there ever been any stretches of time, lasting at least two weeks, where you were completely free of those heavy, depressed feelings, but the voice and the suspicion about the cameras were still happening?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There was a stretch of several weeks when my mood had lifted some and I was getting through meals and work a little better, but I still heard my name in the stairwell and stayed convinced the hallway cameras were being used to track me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if there were periods of at least two weeks where psychotic symptoms (voice and camera suspicions) persisted in the absence of depressive symptoms, which corresponds directly to Criterion B of schizoaffective disorder.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, exactly, Dr. Smith. It's just like I was mentioning a little bit ago when we first started talking today... you're hitting the nail right on the head, or maybe I'm just repeating myself, but yes. 

There was that specific stretch of several weeks—definitely more than two weeks, I'd say closer to three or maybe even four—where my mood had actually lifted some. I remember it clear as day because it was just such a tremendous relief not to feel like I was dragging a hundred-pound weight chained to my ankle every time I had to walk down the corridor. I was getting through my meals, actually eating that turkey sandwich I told you about instead of just tossing it in the bin, and I was getting through my work a little better, too. The floor buffer didn't feel nearly as heavy, and I wasn't dreading the start of my shift the way I usually do. 

But—and this is the part that really just baffles me, I've spent hours thinking about it while I'm wiping down the baseboards—even though I wasn't feeling that awful, crushing depression, the other things didn't stop. I still heard my name in the stairwell. Just as loud and clear as ever, echoing off the concrete. And I stayed absolutely convinced that those hallway cameras were being used to track me. 

I'd be feeling fine, you know, relatively speaking, maybe even looking forward to going back to my apartment and putting my feet up, but I'd look up at that little black dome on the ceiling near the science labs, and I just knew... I knew in my bones that whoever was on the other side of that lens was following my cart. I could feel the motors in the camera adjusting to keep me in the frame. So, to answer your question, yes, there was absolutely a time, for several weeks there, where the heavy, empty feelings took a vacation, but the voice and the cameras didn't go anywhere at all. They just stayed right there on shift with me, completely uninterrupted. It’s a very strange place to be in mentally, I have to tell you, feeling okay but still having all that going on around you.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has ever experienced a distinct period of mania or hypomania, which would help differentiate between Schizoaffective Disorder and Schizophrenia.
doctor.question: During your life, have you ever had any periods lasting at least a few days where you felt unusually energetic, didn't need much sleep, or felt so wired and 'on top of the world' that it was clearly different from your normal self?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of mania or hypomania (e.g., feeling unusually energetic, decreased need for sleep, feeling wired or 'on top of the world'), but there is no such symptom in my profile.

patient.answer:
Well, Dr. Smith, I can tell you right now, 'on top of the world' is definitely not a phrase anybody would ever use to describe me. Not even way back when I was younger, taking those business administration classes at the community college before I started doing the maintenance work. I mean... unusually energetic? I honestly don't think I've ever felt like that in my entire life. 

You ask about not needing much sleep, and, well, I wish I had that problem sometimes! Working the night shift, your sleep schedule gets all turned around and chopped up anyway. I usually try to get my solid seven or eight hours during the day, pulling the blackout curtains tight—I actually went out and bought these heavy-duty ones, the thick kind they use in those nice hotels downtown, because the morning sun just cuts right through my bedroom window and heats up the whole room. But even with those curtains, I'm just always tired. 

I've never had a time where I felt wired, or where I didn't need to sleep for days on end. My baseline is pretty much just... steady, slow, and worn out. Especially with my bad knees. Pushing that heavy supply cart around all night, hauling the giant industrial trash bags out to the main dumpsters behind the cafeteria... it takes every ounce of energy I have just to get through it. There's no bouncing off the walls for me, no big bursts of energy where I feel like I can conquer the world or anything like that. It's really just the exact opposite, like we were talking about before with that heavy, wet blanket feeling. So, no, I can safely say I’ve never experienced anything even close to what you're describing there. Just a whole lot of exhaustion, plain and simple.

inference.note: The patient's report of experiencing clear psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations and delusions of reference) for several weeks in the absence of a mood episode, combined with the fact that his depressive symptoms have been present for the majority of the 11-month duration of his illness, points toward Schizoaffective Disorder. F20.0 (Paranoid Schizophrenia) is less likely given the prominent and persistent mood component. F20.81 (Schizophreniform Disorder) remains a consideration if the total duration of the illness were shorter, but given the 11-month duration, it is less fitting than a chronic diagnosis.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has ever had a psychotic episode independent of mood symptoms that lasted for a significant period (specifically two weeks or more) to distinguish between Schizoaffective Disorder and Schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Aside from the stretch of time you mentioned earlier, have there been any other periods in your life, lasting at least two weeks, where you experienced these voices or suspicious thoughts about the cameras while your mood was completely normal?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if there were any other periods of psychotic symptoms without mood symptoms. The patient's profile only mentions the one specific stretch of several weeks (already discussed under additional_requirement_3), and does not contain information about any other such periods.

patient.answer:
Well, let me really think back on that, Dr. Smith, because I do like to give you the most accurate answer I can. I spend a lot of time thinking about my life while I'm working. You know, when you're just walking up and down those long corridors, back and forth with the floor buffer, you have a lot of time to just chew on your own thoughts. 

And if I'm looking back over my whole life... no, I really don't think so. Because, like I was saying earlier, all this strange business—the voice in the stairwell, the absolute certainty about those dome cameras tracking my cart—all of that really only started up about eleven months ago, right around that awful move to the smaller apartment. Before that... well, I mean, I was always tired, sure, and my knees have been giving me grief for the better part of a decade from all the standing and hauling, but I never heard anyone calling my name when the halls were empty. And I certainly didn't pay any mind to the security cameras back then. I'd just dust the lenses if they got cobwebs on them and keep right on moving. 

So, since the strange things only started eleven months ago, I only have that window of time to look at. And in these past eleven months, it really was just that one specific stretch I told you about—those three or four weeks where the heavy, empty feeling took a vacation but the cameras and the voice stayed on shift. I've racked my brain, going back and forth over the calendar in my head while I'm emptying the recycling bins, trying to remember if maybe there was another time, maybe over the winter holidays? But no. It was just that one time. 

Every other day since this all began, if the voice is there, and if the cameras are watching me, that wet blanket of sadness and guilt is right there with them, wrapped around my shoulders. They've all just been bundled up together, day in and day out. I really wish there had been other times, I'll tell you that much, because feeling somewhat normal in your mood, even if you're terrified the cameras are following you, is a heck of a lot better than feeling so weighed down you can barely lift your arms to tie a trash bag... but no, just that one time.

inference.note: The patient reports a period of at least two weeks of psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations and delusions of being watched) occurring in the absence of a major depressive episode, which is a required criterion for schizoaffective disorder, depressive type. The patient denies ever experiencing a manic or hypomanic episode, ruling out F25.0.
